vignette:
Karim

Karim is a 40-year-old paramedic of Lebanese descent who has been working emergency services for nearly fifteen years. His colleagues describe him as steady under pressure - the kind of man who can thread an IV in the back of a moving rig without flinching. His wife, Nadia, has always said the same thing: that he is the calm one, the one who holds everything together. That reputation feels like a weight to him now.

Fourteen months ago, Karim's younger brother, Samir, collapsed at a family gathering. It was a Sunday afternoon in late autumn, the kind of day full of food and noise and children running between rooms. Karim was standing in the kitchen when he heard his mother scream. He turned to find Samir on the floor, unresponsive, his lips already beginning to blue. Cardiac arrest. Karim knew exactly what to do - he had done it hundreds of times - and yet something inside him fractured in the seconds before his training took over. He began CPR on his own brother, counting compressions on a chest he had known since childhood, calling Samir's name between breaths as if his voice alone could reach him. The ambulance arrived eleven minutes later. Samir survived, but he sustained significant hypoxic brain injury and now lives in a rehabilitation facility. He recognizes almost no one.

In the weeks that followed, Karim returned to work. He told himself this was the right thing - routine, purpose, forward motion. But the rig became something else. The smell of sweat and latex, the particular pitch of a cardiac monitor, the weight of a body going still beneath his hands - these things began to carry Samir inside them. He would be working a call, fully present, and then a detail would land wrong: a patient's age, the color of a shirt, the sound of a family member crying in a hallway. His chest would lock. He would finish the call, but afterward he would sit in the parking bay behind the station and stare at his hands for long minutes before he could make himself go back inside.

At home, he is quieter than he used to be. Nadia notices, though she is careful about how she names it. He sleeps poorly, waking at two or three in the morning with a vague, crushing sense of dread that he cannot always trace back to a specific dream. Sometimes the dream is explicit - he is doing compressions and Samir opens his eyes but does not know him - and he wakes with his heart hammering, needing a moment to remember where he is. He has stopped going to his parents' house on Sundays. The living room where it happened is unremarkable in every way, and that unremarkableness is somehow the worst part.

He carries a specific and persistent guilt that he has not spoken aloud to anyone. He is a paramedic. He has saved strangers. He tells himself that those eleven minutes were not his fault, that he did everything correctly, and then he does not believe himself. He wonders whether he hesitated, whether some part of him froze in a way he has since edited out of the memory. He replays the sequence looking for the moment he failed, and the sequence never resolves.

He describes himself as someone who is managing. He comes to sessions neatly dressed, answers questions directly, and occasionally makes a dry joke about the particular absurdity of a paramedic needing help with medical trauma. Beneath that composure, though, he is a man who has not been back to visit his brother in three months, because sitting across from Samir's empty gaze and knowing that his hands were the last thing between that man and the life he had - that is the thing Karim does not yet know how to carry.
